quote.text:
Alright I'm done dude.  Today changed the entire AI game again.  Throwing my Mac mini in the trash. Deleting all my subs and just maxing out Grok Bot.

You don't need anything else anymore. I made this video by opening Grok Bot, and spending about 15 seconds writing the following prompt:

"Make me an explainer video on the natural gas supply chain for residential service, from where gas is generated to the delivery line into your home. Talk about how pressure is stepped down at each stop along the way, how lines are run, etc"

Grok Bot is just a magic box that you write a little bit of English into and get out gold. I'm done with everything else.  I don't care anymore.

My goal with these videos is to help people understand that the simplest things they take for granted are actually very complex, and you should be amazed by everything basically.

Elon Musk was set to spend 1995 at Stanford working on the biggest problem holding back electric cars. Then he walked into his professor's office.

"Bill Nix would have been my professor. He's the guy I spoke to when I said... I'd like to put my studies on hold... And he's like, sure, but I don't think I'm gonna hear from you again. And that was the last conversation I had with Bill Nix." @elonmusk

What was he going to study? "How to solve the energy density problem for electric vehicles."

What if he had stayed at Stanford?

posts.author: elonmusk
posts.text:
In April 2009, Elon Musk was asked why General Motors wouldn't just buy Tesla. 

"You can't afford it." 

Fifty-five days later, GM was bankrupt.

He was 37, and his salary was $1.

In late 2007 his own car cost $140,000 to build. Tesla was selling it for $92,000, a $48,000 hole in every car, with the money almost gone.

November 2008: GM's Rick Wagoner flew to Washington on a $36 million corporate jet to ask Congress for $10 to 12 billion. A congressman asked him if he would work for $1 a year. Wagoner, paid $15.7 million in 2007, said he had no position on that today.

The clip is two moments from one evening at Silicon Valley's Churchill Club. In the first, Musk admits how close Tesla came to running out of money. In the second, he explains Detroit.

"Tesla was in a really dire situation at the end of 2007."

"This was inevitable. It was only a question of when."

That is Musk on April 7, 2009, four weeks after the stock market hit its crisis low and fourteen months before Tesla went public at $17 a share.

The money rules in that talk fit on an index card.

Know your floor before you need it. At 17, with a few thousand dollars, he tested whether he could live on under $1 a day, hot dogs and oranges bought in bulk.

Set the first target at groceries. Zip2 was started to cover food. It sold for over $300 million.

Learn the money side, or someone else decides for you. That is why a physics student also took an economics degree at Wharton.

If rent eats the business, cut the rent. He and his brother slept on futons in the office and showered at the YMCA.

Know your unit cost before you scale. That $48,000 hole nearly ended Tesla.

GM's bill went to the public: a $49.5 billion rescue, and $11.2 billion of it never came back to taxpayers.

In the same talk Musk said he would love to take over NUMMI, the GM and Toyota plant in Fremont, but couldn't afford it unless someone gave it to him. GM walked away from the plant in bankruptcy. Tesla bought it the next year for $42 million.

The full 93-minute talk is free on YouTube. In 17 years it has gathered about 333,000 views.

GM had billions of public money and still walked away from the factory. Musk started with one number: how little he could live on. Work out yours before you quit a paycheck.

I just turned my own comment section into a full-color Japanese manga using Grok Bot. So if you replied to my CFO post, you might actually be in a comic book now.

Grok Bot can now search, read, and monitor 𝕏, so I quote reposted that post and tagged @bot with one request…
read the replies and turn the whole conversation into a manga. It went through around 477 replies and quote posts, picked out the funniest comments, and turned the arguments into battles.

Being able to read what people are actually saying on 𝕏 opens up some pretty fun possibilities beyond asking a bot questions.

Tag @bot on one of your posts and try it. 

Super cool feature.

posts.author: elonmusk
posts.text:
For nearly FIVE YEARS, Elon and the Starlink team have been trying to bring high-speed internet to India, especially to rural and remote areas where reliable connectivity is still difficult and expensive to reach

Starlink has spent years working through India’s requirements

It has secured its telecom licences, received IN-SPACe approval, built 20+ gateway sites and designed its operations specifically around India’s security requirements including keeping Indian user data inside India

And yet Starlink still cannot serve a single commercial customer

The final clearances and spectrum assignment are still pending

India is still about 64% rural…..roughly 941 million people live in rural areas

Starlink is ready
The ground infrastructure is already built

That years-long delay is hard to justify and incredibly frustrating

Starlink will give many more people another way to access high-speed internet, especially in places where fibre and mobile networks struggle to reach

And that makes the situation even harder to understand when Digital India itself is built around broadband access and closing connectivity gaps

If the goal is really to bring more Indians online, Starlink should not still be sitting on the sidelines after nearly five years

posts.author: elonmusk
posts.text:
Elon Musk on why internet access is one of the most powerful tools humanity has for lifting people out of poverty:

“The single biggest thing you can do to lift people out of poverty and help them is giving them an internet connection”

Because once someone gets connected, their opportunities completely change

• they can learn almost anything for free
• get access education and information
• Find work and build businesses
• Sell goods and services to the global market
• Participate in an economy far beyond their local community

That is the bigger mission behind Starlink

Bringing low-cost, high-bandwidth internet to places where traditional connectivity is unavailable, too expensive or simply never reaches

For hundreds of millions of people, an internet connection is not just a convenience....it is access to new opportunity they never had before https://x.com/XFreeze/status/2015067284205916553/video/1
